name: Botrytis gray mold and bud rot
summary: A destructive Cannabis flower, stem, leaf, seedling, and postharvest disease associated with brown water-soaked or necrotic decay and, when conditions permit, gray to gray-brown sporulation. Internal flower decay can be poorly represented by an exterior view, and brown bud rot is not species-specific without laboratory confirmation.
affectedParts: fan leaves under severe disease pressure
indicators: One or more bracts or sugar leaves within a flower turn water-soaked, tan, or brown and collapse
Brown necrosis and mycelium occur inside a flower when it is carefully opened
Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth or dusty spore masses develop on dead flower or stem tissue under humid conditions
Localized flower decay expands until much or all of an inflorescence is brown, dry-rotted, or collapsed
Stem lesions become pale or brown cankers and may split, girdle, or break; black sclerotia can occur
Under severe late-harvest pressure, small circular leaf spots can enlarge, merge, and become vein-delimited necrotic areas, sometimes with yellow margins
Multiple affected flowers cluster in dense, humid, poorly drying canopy zones and increase on serial inspection
exclusions: White superficial colonies occur without brown internal decay and microscopy supports powdery mildew
Only pistils or evenly aging leaves have browned while bracts, stems, and internal flower tissue remain firm and free of advancing lesions
Fusarium, Penicillium, or another mold is recovered from the active lesion instead of Botrytis
White cottony mycelium and the laboratory result support Sclerotinia rather than Botrytis
Damage stops after a documented heat, light, spray, or mechanical event and no mycelium, spores, or advancing rot develop
Caterpillars, frass, chewing, or webbing explain the localized flower collapse
A single postharvest discoloration image is available without intact-tissue context, environmental history, microscopy, culture, or molecular testing

progression.description: A small water-soaked or brown area develops on bracts, adjacent leaves, or a stem; exterior images can understate internal flower involvement.
Necrosis spreads through nearby bracts and flower tissue, with internal brown decay or mycelium becoming apparent when the affected flower is examined safely.
Gray to gray-brown fuzzy growth and spore masses develop on necrotic tissue; their absence in a dry image does not exclude an earlier or inactive infection.
A large portion or the whole inflorescence can be destroyed, stems can canker or break, and internal decay can persist into harvested material.

lookAlikes: Fusarium flower mold or bud rot
Normal pistil browning and late-flower senescence
Caterpillar or other boring-insect injury with frass
Heat, light, spray, or mechanical injury
confirmation: Capture the affected flower exterior, a safely exposed interior cross-section, a close-up of the active lesion margin, surrounding flowers, and a whole-plant distribution view with scale; do not infer a clean interior from an exterior photograph.

Record serial change plus flowering or harvest stage, canopy location, temperature, relative humidity, condensation or wetness duration, irrigation or rain exposure, air movement, and drying conditions; these variables describe risk but do not confirm the organism.
With appropriate containment and protective procedures, sample the interface between advancing diseased and apparently healthy tissue rather than only dry dead tissue.

Submit representative flower or stem tissue to a plant diagnostic laboratory for microscopy and isolation plus a validated molecular or sequence-based assay when a Botrytis species label matters; request testing that considers Fusarium, Penicillium, Sclerotinia, and other flower molds.

Keep the image label at suspected gray mold or bud rot unless organism evidence is linked to the photographed plant and lesion; morphology or an environmental match alone is not laboratory confirmation.
immediateActions: Isolate or clearly mark suspect plants and stop moving affected flowers, tools, clothing, or debris through clean areas.
Avoid shaking or uncontained opening of visibly sporulating flowers; collect diagnostic images and samples with procedures that limit spore dispersal.
Separate visibly moldy harvested material from apparently clean material and do not consume or distribute it.
correctivePlan: Base crop removal, sanitation, environmental correction, and any treatment on the confirmed diagnosis, current local law, the production system, growth stage, and the current product label.
Reduce persistent tissue wetness and correct airflow or humidity problems documented in the affected zone without treating an environmental adjustment as proof that Botrytis caused the lesion.
Reinspect fixed flowers and neighboring plants over time; document new lesions and laboratory results, because old necrotic tissue will not recover.
prevention: Scout both exterior and protected interior flower zones during flowering and before harvest, especially where tissue dries slowly.
Sanitize tools between plants, remove crop debris without dispersing it, and prevent infected propagation or harvested material from entering clean zones.
Maintain traceable records linking plant, room or field position, media, environmental logs, sample identifier, and laboratory result.
warnings: Brown flower decay, gray fuzz, humidity, or a damaged sugar leaf alone is not species-level ground truth; multiple fungi and noninfectious injuries overlap visually.
Opening diseased flowers can expose hidden decay but can also release spores; use containment and appropriate protective procedures.
Temperature and humidity ranges reported by institutions are conducive-condition context, not universal diagnostic thresholds.

The CC BY composite figure is reference-only pending panel-level annotation and dataset-split review; the three university photographs have no explicit reuse license and remain hidden metadata references.
Do not use or distribute visibly mold-contaminated flower.

sources.title: Pathogens and Molds Affecting Production and Quality of Cannabis sativa L.
sources.organization: Frontiers in Plant Science (Punja et al.)
supportedClaims: Across sampled indoor, greenhouse, and field Cannabis crops, flower buds with brown discoloration, blighted bracts and leaves, tissue decay, and grayish-brown mycelium yielded cultures identified as Botrytis cinerea by morphology and ITS-rDNA sequencing.

The study documented a visual sequence from browning and decay of leaves and bracts in developing inflorescences to destruction of the entire inflorescence, as well as internal mycelium and decay in harvested flowers.

Under severe late-harvest disease pressure, Cannabis leaves developed small circular spots that enlarged and coalesced into necrotic, often vein-delimited areas, sometimes with yellow margins; this leaf presentation was contextual rather than a standalone diagnostic rule.

Botrytis cinerea, Fusarium oxysporum, and Penicillium olsonii recovered from harvested buds each produced browning and decay after inoculation under high humidity, demonstrating that brown bud rot is not species-specific in an image.

Figure 4 is a multi-panel Cannabis reference containing early and advanced inflorescence disease, internal harvested-bud decay, culture and microscopy views, and leaf lesions; the article and figure are licensed CC BY 4.0.

sources.title: Hemp (Cannabis sativa)-Gray Mold (Botrytis Bud Blight and Stem Canker)
sources.publisher: Oregon State University, Washington State University, and University of Idaho
supportedClaims: Gray mold can affect Cannabis seedlings, stems, foliage, and flowers; brown water-soaked bud spots can progress to dead inflorescences covered by brown to gray-brown spores.
Stem infection can produce cankers, splitting or breakage, and black sclerotia, while heavily affected plants can decline quickly under conducive conditions.
Cool, humid or wet conditions and prolonged tissue wetness favor disease, but environmental conditions are risk context rather than proof of cause.

The page photographs show a close exterior bud-rot view, a close sporulating-flower view, and a whole-plant distribution view; each is credited to Cynthia M. Ocamb in 2020, and the page states copyright without an explicit media-reuse license.

sources.title: Gray Mold of Industrial Hemp
supportedClaims: Brown water-soaked lesions on hemp stems, leaves, or flowers can become necrotic and develop gray spores; stem lesions can girdle stems, cause breakage, and form black irregular sclerotia.
Seedlings and cuttings can damp off under cool, wet conditions, with necrotic or water-soaked roots, while moist and humid production conditions favor disease development.

Fusarium flower mold can resemble gray mold but lacks the characteristic gray spore masses, Fusarium cankers lack gray spores and sclerotia, and Sclerotinia produces white mycelial mats; these features guide triage but laboratory confirmation remains appropriate.
